title: Your Nitnem, chosen
hook: write down the daily prayer you will keep
tomorrow: no gurdwara near campus. so where does Simran's seva go?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ways: ragas, teaching, the code, the streams, and one light under all of it, Kabir's line in Simran's speech. Now the looking back turns into choosing.

The housing email lands at dinner: a dorm room, a roommate from another state, and an eight o'clock class. No Bebe across the yard. No chili rows at dawn. Simran reads it out, then asks the question everyone at the table has been waiting for. Which prayers come with me? Bebe answers first: all of them, the whole Nitnem, every day. Her dad puts down his fork. Start with what you'll actually keep.
screen: `A DORM, A ROOMMATE, AN EARLY CLASS.` → `WHICH PRAYERS COME WITH ME?` → `ALL OF THEM, OR WHAT YOU'LL KEEP?`

segments.voice: Nitnem is the daily rule of prayer. Guru Ram Das paints the picture on Ang 305, paraphrased: one who calls themselves a Sikh of the Guru rises early and keeps the Name in mind. The Sikh code, the Rehat Maryada, names the banis: the Japji, the Jaap and others at dawn, Rehras in the evening, Sohila at night. Some families and groups add more. So here are the two views at Simran's table, and both are real. Bebe's: a rule is a rule because it doesn't bend to your mood. Keep the Nitnem whole, on tired days and busy ones, and the keeping becomes the practice. If you trim it whenever life gets loud, life will always be loud. Harjit's: a rule you break by week two teaches you that you break rules. Start with what you can keep every single day, the Japji at dawn and Sohila at night, and grow toward the whole. Bebe says that's how habits shrink. Harjit says that's how they last. Simran listens to both of them for a long time. Then she gets a pen and a sticky note, and writes the first line of her Nitnem, the one she'll keep in a dorm with a sleeping roommate.
screen: `ANG 305: RISE EARLY, KEEP THE NAME.` · `THE CODE NAMES THE BANIS.` · `KEEP IT WHOLE, WHATEVER THE MOOD.` · `KEEP WHAT YOU CAN, AND GROW.` · then, large: `MY NITNEM.`

segments.voice: On paper, write the daily prayer you'll keep: which bani, what time, where you'll be. Make it something you could keep on your worst day, and if you're aiming for more, write that underneath. Read it back to yourself once, slowly.
Your Nitnem: the daily rule of prayer, chosen by you and written down, whole or growing toward whole.
Pocket this: my nitnem, written down where I'll see it at dawn. One sticky note, already on the mirror.

screen: `DAY 1774 COUNTS.` → `THE SUMMIT · 14 OF 31.` → `TOMORROW: NO GURDWARA NEAR CAMPUS. WHERE DOES SEVA GO?`

howItsDone: Sikhs keep Nitnem by reciting set banis each day, the Japji and others in the morning, Rehras in the evening and Sohila at night, often from a gutka; some recite from memory, some listen to recordings, and some families and groups include more banis.

fork.setup: you lean toward starting small. a friend asks you to give the best case for keeping the full Nitnem from day one. what do you say?
options: a rule that never bends to your mood trains you; keeping it whole is the practice.
the full Nitnem earns more blessing per minute than a short prayer ever could.
a shorter Nitnem doesn't count at all, so there's no point starting with one.
fork.reveal: the strongest case for the whole Nitnem is about steadiness: a rule kept on tired and busy days becomes the practice. the other two are not what either side says.

chat.says: bebe says full nitnem or it doesn't count. dad says start with what i'll keep. help??
options: both are real views. write down what you'll keep daily, and the whole you're aiming for.
dad's right. the code is only a suggestion, so any prayer counts the same.
bebe's right. if you can't do the whole thing, skip it until you can.
chat.meaning: Bebe's case is steadiness: a whole rule kept on hard days. Harjit's is a rule you can keep, then grow. Simran writes hers down.

Nitnem.meaning: the daily rule of set Sikh prayers

Sohila.meaning: the Sikh prayer said before sleep
